s: When a company enters a competitive market with strong capital, advanced technology, and experienced management. When a student prepares thoroughly for an important exam with complete study materials and deep knowledge of the subject matter.

l: wrapped in coarse cloth yet harboring jade
m: A person of noble character or talent who lives humbly and does not display their worth outwardly.
s: When someone you know is extremely talented or virtuous but dresses plainly and doesn't boast about their abilities. When a colleague with a humble demeanor turns out to be exceptionally skilled or intelligent. When you discover that a quiet, unassuming person has remarkable hidden talents or moral integrity.

l: dress up in false appearance and adopt false manner
m: To pretend to be something one is not by adopting a fake appearance or manner in order to deceive others.
s: When someone acts prim and proper around authority figures but behaves completely differently with friends. When a coworker suddenly starts speaking formally and acting refined just because the boss walked into the room, even though everyone knows they're not really like that.

m: to focus on superficial appearance and presentation while neglecting substance or inner quality.
s: When a company spends money on fancy office decorations but pays employees poorly. When someone buys expensive clothes to impress others but has no real skills or character. When a restaurant has beautiful decor but serves terrible food.

l: Pretend to be crazy and sell stupidity
m: To deliberately act foolish or insane in order to deceive others or avoid responsibility.
s: When someone pretends not to understand something obvious to get out of trouble. When a person acts like they don't know how to do a task so they don't have to do it. When someone feigns ignorance or mental incapacity to avoid being held accountable for their actions.

l: pretend to be deaf and mute
m: To deliberately ignore or refuse to acknowledge something by pretending not to hear or understand it.
s: When someone ignores your repeated requests and acts like they didn't hear you. When a person refuses to engage with a difficult topic by pretending they don't know what you're talking about.

l: put on an appearance and make gestures
m: To affect a pretentious manner or put on airs in order to impress others or seem more important than one actually is.
s: When someone tries to act sophisticated or important around people they want to impress, even though it's clearly fake. When a coworker suddenly changes their behavior and speaks differently when the boss walks into the room.

m: To be held back by fear or self-imposed limitations and refuse to move forward.
s: When someone is too afraid or embarrassed to try something new, even though they really want to. When a person lets their own doubts and insecurity prevent them from pursuing an opportunity or taking a risk.

l: chest and mind transparent and white
m: To be completely honest, sincere, and open-hearted with no hidden thoughts or deceptive intentions.
s: When someone admits their mistakes freely without making excuses. When a friend tells you the truth about a difficult situation even though it might hurt your feelings. When a person shares their genuine feelings and thoughts without pretense or manipulation.

m: To communicate important ideas in a concise and efficient manner without unnecessary elaboration.
s: When a speaker delivers a powerful presentation without wasting time on irrelevant details. When someone writes a clear email that gets straight to the point instead of rambling on. When instructions are given briefly but cover everything that needs to be said.

p: fù cháo zhī xià wú wán luǎn
l: Beneath a destroyed nest, no egg remains whole
m: When a disaster affects a group or organization, no one within it can escape the consequences; individual safety depends on the collective stability.
s: When a company goes bankrupt, all employees lose their jobs regardless of their individual performance. When a country is invaded, ordinary citizens suffer along with everyone else, even if they personally did nothing wrong.

l: spilled water cannot be gathered back
m: Once something is done, it cannot be undone; past actions have irreversible consequences.
s: When someone realizes they said something hurtful to a friend and can never take back those words. When a person makes a big mistake at work and wishes they could undo it, but they know the damage is already done.

m: To act bravely and without hesitation to defend what is right or help someone in danger.
s: When someone jumps into a dangerous situation to help a stranger in trouble. When a person speaks up against injustice even though it might cost them something. When a bystander intervenes to stop wrongdoing instead of walking away.

m: Different people have different perspectives and interpretations based on their own values and understanding.
s: When a movie receives mixed reviews because viewers interpret it differently. When colleagues disagree on the best approach to solve a problem, each thinking their solution is most reasonable. When people debate a controversial topic and each person holds a different but defensible viewpoint.

m: To abandon one's principles and moral integrity in pursuit of personal gain or money.
s: When a trusted employee steals from the company for a small bonus. When a friend betrays your confidence to gain favor with someone more popular or wealthy.

l: having seen much and known much
m: Having extensive experience and broad knowledge acquired through exposure to many different things and situations.
s: When someone gives you advice because they've traveled to many countries and lived through different experiences. When an older colleague at work can solve problems quickly because they've dealt with similar situations many times before.

l: seeing something different, thinking of changing
m: To be fickle and easily distracted by new things, abandoning loyalty or commitment when something more appealing appears.
s: When someone leaves their partner as soon as they meet someone new. When an employee quits their job the moment a slightly better opportunity comes along, without loyalty to their current company.

l: See the small and know the great
m: By observing small signs or details, one can infer or predict larger truths, trends, or consequences that will follow.
s: When a company's customer service starts declining, you can predict bigger problems are coming. When you notice a friend becoming withdrawn and quiet, you sense deeper emotional issues developing. When early sales figures suggest a product won't succeed in the market.

l: see strangeness without finding it strange
m: To encounter something unusual or shocking but treat it as completely normal and unremarkable.
s: When you've lived in a chaotic city for so long that traffic jams and loud noises no longer bother you. When a doctor sees so many unusual medical cases that nothing surprises them anymore. When someone has experienced so much drama in their life that even bizarre situations don't faze them.

p: jiàn suǒ wèi jiàn ， wén suǒ wèi wén
l: see what has not been seen, hear what has not been heard
m: To witness or experience something entirely novel and unprecedented that exceeds one's previous knowledge or imagination.
s: When you travel to a foreign country and encounter completely unfamiliar customs and traditions. When a new technology is introduced that revolutionizes how people work in ways nobody had experienced before.

l: observe the opportunity and act accordingly
m: Adapt your actions based on the current circumstances and opportunities rather than following a fixed plan.
s: When a salesman changes his pitch depending on whether the customer seems interested or skeptical. When a teacher adjusts the lesson difficulty based on how well students are understanding the material. When someone decides whether to speak up or stay quiet depending on the mood of the group.

l: see the object but not the person
m: To focus only on material things or external matters while ignoring or neglecting the people involved, or to be so absorbed in objects that one overlooks human relationships and connections.
s: When someone is so focused on accumulating wealth and possessions that they neglect their family and friends. When a manager obsesses over production numbers and efficiency metrics but ignores the well-being and concerns of their employees.

l: seeing hunting makes the heart happy
m: One's latent passion or talent is suddenly awakened upon encountering something that stirs one's interest or skill.
s: When someone who used to play an instrument sees others performing and suddenly feels the urge to pick it back up. When a retired athlete watches a game and feels that old competitive fire returning to their heart.

l: see a crack and insert a needle
m: To make use of every tiny opportunity or spare moment, no matter how small, to accomplish something.
s: When someone squeezes in exercise or study sessions whenever they have a few free minutes throughout their day. When a person manages to fit in a quick conversation or task whenever there's a brief gap in their busy schedule.

m: To change one's position or opinion opportunistically based on circumstances rather than holding firm to principles.
s: When a politician changes their stance depending on what's popular at the moment. When a colleague suddenly agrees with the boss's idea even though they disagreed with it before. When someone abandons their beliefs just because the situation has changed.

m: Standards, principles, and guidelines that establish proper conduct and boundaries for behavior.
s: When a company establishes clear policies for how employees should conduct themselves. When parents set household rules to teach children what is and isn't acceptable behavior. When a community has established norms about how people should treat each other respectfully.

l: walk by rule and step by square
m: To conduct oneself with strict propriety and adherence to established rules and moral standards.
s: When someone always follows the rules perfectly and never takes shortcuts or breaks from tradition. When describing a person who is very proper, formal, and always does things the correct way without any deviation.

m: to view something as extremely difficult, dangerous, or daunting, and therefore avoid or be reluctant to undertake it.
s: When someone is afraid to start a new job because they think it will be too hard. When a student avoids taking a challenging class because they're intimidated by the subject matter.

m: To consider someone as your closest friend or soulmate with whom you share a deep mutual understanding and trust.
s: When you meet someone who completely understands you and shares your values, so you immediately feel like you've known them forever. When two people have such compatible personalities that they become each other's most trusted confidant and closest companion.

m: To treat something serious with a lack of respect or responsibility, as if it were merely child's play.
s: When someone doesn't take an important project seriously and just goofs around instead of doing the work. When a student treats their final exam like a joke and doesn't study at all.

m: To treat someone as if they are a complete stranger, ignoring their past relationship or connection.
s: When two former friends have a falling out and now pretend not to know each other. When someone deliberately ignores a person they used to be close to because of a conflict or betrayal.

m: To treat someone with extreme hostility and contempt, as if they were a mortal enemy.
s: When a parent completely disowns their child and refuses to acknowledge them. When two former friends become so angry that they treat each other with absolute disdain and animosity.

m: To treat something or someone with complete contempt and disregard, viewing them as utterly worthless.
s: When someone dismisses another person's hard work or accomplishments without any respect. When a wealthy person ignores the value of money because they have so much of it. When someone treats a gift or kind gesture as if it means absolutely nothing.

m: To face death with complete fearlessness and acceptance, treating it as a natural or even welcome outcome.
s: When a soldier charges into battle knowing the odds are against survival. When someone stands up for their principles even though it will cost them their life. When a martyr accepts execution rather than renounce their beliefs.

m: To deliberately ignore something that is obvious or right in front of you.
s: When your friend is clearly upset but you pretend not to notice and don't ask what's wrong. When a manager knows about a serious problem at work but chooses to ignore it and do nothing about it.

p: shì ér bù jiàn ， tīng ér bú wén
l: see but do not perceive, hear but do not understand
m: To deliberately ignore or refuse to acknowledge something that is obvious or that one is aware of.
s: When someone pretends not to notice a problem even though it's right in front of them. When a parent ignores their child's repeated requests for help with homework. When a coworker acts oblivious to the mess they created in the shared office space.

m: To deliberately ignore or pretend not to notice something that is obvious or right in front of you.
s: When your partner leaves dirty dishes everywhere and you just ignore them instead of confronting the issue. When a manager sees an employee making mistakes but does nothing about it. When you notice your friend is upset but pretend not to notice and change the subject.

m: To generously give money or financial assistance to help someone in need.
s: When a friend is struggling financially and you offer to lend or give them money. When a wealthy person donates a large sum to help a charity or community in crisis.

m: To free oneself from rigid, outdated, or restrictive ways of thinking in order to embrace new ideas and perspectives.
s: When a company needs to abandon old business practices and adopt innovative strategies to stay competitive. When a student realizes they've been limiting themselves with self-doubt and decides to pursue ambitious goals they previously thought impossible.

l: remove armor and return to the fields
m: to retire from military service or public office and return to a peaceful life of farming or simple living.
s: When a soldier retires after decades of service and decides to go back to his hometown to farm. When a government official steps down from their position and chooses to live a quiet life in the countryside instead of pursuing more power.

l: untie the bell, tie the bell
m: The person who created a problem is the one best suited to solve it.
s: When a coworker caused a mistake in a project and you expect them to fix it rather than someone else. When two friends had a falling out and you think they should be the ones to reconcile with each other, not a third party trying to mediate.

m: The sight of a particular place or scene evokes deep emotions or memories.
s: When you visit a childhood home and suddenly feel nostalgic or sad. When you see a familiar location that reminds you of someone you've lost or a significant event from your past.

l: touch the eye and alarm the heart
m: Something is so shocking or distressing that it immediately strikes fear and distress upon seeing it.
s: When you walk into a room and see a terrible accident or injury that horrifies you at first sight. When news footage of a disaster is so graphic and disturbing that it deeply shocks viewers. When you discover evidence of terrible mistreatment or neglect that deeply upsets you.

l: wherever the eye touches, all are present
m: Something is so common or widespread that it is visible everywhere you look.
s: When you walk through a city and see homeless people on every street corner. When a company's advertisements appear in every store, on every billboard, and on every website you visit.

l: touch one category and extend to the sides
m: By understanding one principle or mastering one skill, you can apply that knowledge to understand or master many related things.
s: When a student learns one math concept and suddenly understands how to solve many similar problems. When someone picks up one musical instrument and finds it easy to learn another because they understand the underlying principles. When a person grasps one aspect of their job and can quickly figure out related tasks without being taught.

m: Speaking in a way that lacks substance, purpose, or meaningful content; indulging in shallow or trivial talk.
s: When someone talks a lot but says nothing important or useful. When a person gives a long speech that sounds impressive but has no real point or value.

l: words not proceeding from the heart
m: To say things that do not reflect one's true feelings or beliefs; to speak insincerely.
s: When someone apologizes but you can tell they don't really mean it. When a politician gives a speech that sounds nice but you know they don't actually care about the issues they're discussing.

l: Words are the voice of the heart
m: What people say truly reflects their inner thoughts and feelings.
s: When someone's words reveal their true intentions or emotions that they were trying to hide. When you notice that despite someone claiming to be fine, their words betray their real sadness or anger.

m: Speaking with absolute certainty and conviction, presenting statements as if they are indisputable facts.
s: When someone makes bold claims about something without any doubt or hesitation. When a person insists their version of events is 100% true even though you weren't there to verify it. When someone speaks with such confidence that you might believe them even if you have doubts.

m: Speech that is logical, well-founded, and persuasive, with sound reasoning behind every point.
s: When someone presents an argument that makes perfect sense and you can't find any faults with their logic. When a colleague explains their project proposal so clearly and convincingly that everyone agrees it's a solid plan.

m: Speech or writing that contains no meaningful content, ideas, or value.
s: When someone gives a long speech but doesn't actually say anything important or concrete. When a student writes a lot of words in an essay but doesn't make any real points or arguments.

l: Words of each person are different
m: Everyone has their own perspective, opinion, or way of expressing things, and these naturally vary from person to person.
s: When you ask five people about the same event and they all describe it differently based on what they noticed. When a group of colleagues interprets company policy in different ways based on their own understanding.

l: instruction by words and teaching by example
m: To educate others through both verbal instruction and personal example, with actions being as important as words.
s: When a parent teaches their child not to lie but then lies themselves, they're not practicing 言传身教. A good teacher practices 言传身教 by being punctual, respectful, and hardworking while also explaining these values to their students. When a coach tells athletes to stay fit but shows up overweight, that's a failure of 言传身教.

m: A person's words are so authoritative and powerful that they are instantly obeyed like laws, often describing someone with absolute power or influence.
s: When a powerful leader or boss speaks and everyone immediately follows their orders without question. When someone is so respected and influential that their suggestions are treated as commands that must be obeyed.

m: To obey someone completely and follow their advice without any hesitation or question.
s: When an employee does exactly what their boss tells them without thinking for themselves. When a child listens to every instruction their parent gives and never argues or resists.

m: The hidden or implied message that lies beneath what is explicitly stated.
s: When someone says they're 'fine' but you can tell from their tone they're actually upset. When a person agrees to something verbally but their body language suggests they really don't want to do it.

m: After a conflict or disagreement, two people reconcile and restore their friendly relationship.
s: When two friends have been arguing but finally apologize and make up. When a couple has had a big fight but decides to work things out and get back together.

l: words return to the proper transmission
m: to stop digressing and return to the main topic or subject being discussed.
s: When someone has been telling a long story full of tangents and finally says 'anyway, back to what I was saying.' When a teacher pauses a lesson to refocus the class after everyone got distracted by a side conversation.

p: yán bì xìn ， xíng bì guǒ
l: Words must be trustworthy, actions must be fruitful
m: One should always keep their promises and follow through on their commitments with decisive action.
s: When someone consistently does what they say they will do, you can trust them completely. When a leader makes promises and then takes concrete steps to fulfill them. When evaluating whether someone is reliable and dependable in their word and actions.

m: Whatever one says is always pertinent, appropriate, and strikes at the heart of the matter.
s: When someone always knows exactly what to say in any situation and their comments are always spot-on and relevant. When a person has such good judgment that their advice or observations are consistently accurate and meaningful.

l: Words still linger in the ear
m: Someone's words are still fresh in one's memory and have not been forgotten.
s: When your boss just gave you important instructions a moment ago and you're still thinking about what they said. When a friend made a promise recently and you're reminding them that their words are still fresh in your mind.

m: Using few words to express complete and profound meaning; being brief yet comprehensive.
s: When a teacher explains a complex concept in just a few clear sentences that perfectly captures everything you need to know. When someone writes a short email that says exactly what needs to be said without any unnecessary details.

p: yán zhě wú zuì ， wén zhě zú jiè
l: The speaker is blameless, the listener should be warned
m: When someone gives frank criticism or advice, they should not be blamed for speaking up, and the listener should take the criticism seriously as a lesson rather than hold a grudge against the speaker.
s: When a coworker points out a mistake you made in a project and you feel offended, but then realize they were just trying to help you improve. When a family member gives you honest feedback about your behavior that stings at first, but you later recognize it was valuable advice meant for your own good.

m: Someone who says things but fails to follow through on their promises or commitments.
s: When a coworker promises to help with a project but never shows up. When a politician makes campaign promises but doesn't keep them after winning. When a friend repeatedly says they'll call you back but never does.

m: To say what you mean and follow through on your promises; to be a person of integrity whose word can be relied upon.
s: When someone consistently does what they say they will do, you can trust them completely. When a friend always keeps their promises and never breaks their word, no matter the circumstances.

m: One's actions match what one says; there is no discrepancy between words and deeds.
s: When someone does exactly what they promised to do. When you trust a person because they always follow through on their commitments. When evaluating whether a politician's behavior matches their campaign promises.

l: words and actions are not one
m: A person's words do not match their actions; they say one thing but do another.
s: When a politician campaigns on fighting corruption but then takes bribes once elected. When a friend promises to help you move but never shows up. When a company advertises they care about the environment but continues polluting.

m: To exaggerate or overstate something beyond what is actually true.
s: When someone describes their accomplishments in a way that sounds much more impressive than they actually are. When a salesman makes claims about a product that are clearly more dramatic than what it can actually do.

l: words are near but meaning is far
m: Simple or plain language conceals a deep or profound message that extends far beyond the surface meaning.
s: When a teacher uses a short, simple story to teach an important life lesson. When someone gives brief advice that seems ordinary at first but contains wisdom you only understand later. When a mentor makes a casual comment that turns out to be much more meaningful than you initially realized.

l: swear that both cannot stand together
m: Two parties are sworn enemies who cannot coexist and are determined to destroy each other.
s: When two rival companies are in a cutthroat competition where one must completely defeat the other to survive. When two people have such deep hatred for each other that they vow they can never be reconciled or live in peace together.

m: To vow that one will not stop or give up until a goal is achieved or a wrong is righted.
s: When someone is determined to keep fighting for justice until they win their case. When an athlete refuses to quit training until they finally break a world record. When a person keeps pursuing a dream no matter how many times they fail.

m: To pledge unwavering loyalty and commitment to someone or something, even at the cost of one's life.
s: When someone demonstrates absolute dedication to a cause or person despite facing serious dangers or hardships. When a loyal friend refuses to abandon you no matter what difficulties arise. When a soldier or follower shows unshakeable allegiance to their leader or principles.

m: To mark progress by counting the days and measuring the work completed each day, emphasizing diligent effort and steady advancement toward a goal.
s: When a student is preparing for an exam and tracking their daily study progress to ensure they cover all material in time. When a project manager breaks down a large task into daily goals and monitors completion to stay on schedule.

m: to treat an enemy or oppressor as a benefactor, or to be so deceived that you regard a harmful person as a savior.
s: When someone is manipulated by a dishonest person and mistakenly trusts them as if they were family. When people are so oppressed that they begin to admire or respect their oppressor without realizing the harm being done to them.

m: To negotiate or bargain over the terms or price of a deal, typically by making counteroffers back and forth.
s: When you're buying a used car and going back and forth with the seller over the asking price. When a customer and shopkeeper are negotiating the final cost of an item at a market. When two parties are trying to reach a compromise on the terms of a business agreement.

m: To flatter and ingratiate oneself with others in order to gain their approval or advantage.
s: When someone is constantly complimenting their boss and acting overly helpful just to get a promotion. When a person pretends to be innocent and well-behaved around authority figures but acts differently when no one important is watching.

m: Someone or a group has received thorough training and preparation, demonstrating skill, discipline, and competence in their actions.
s: When you watch a military unit move in perfect coordination during a ceremony. When a sports team executes plays flawlessly because they practice constantly. When a professional team handles a crisis calmly because they've drilled the procedures many times.

m: An event or experience remains vivid and clear in one's mind as if it happened recently.
s: When you clearly remember something that happened not too long ago and can recall all the details. When a friend reminds you of an embarrassing moment from last year and you remember it perfectly like it just happened yesterday.

l: hide illness and avoid the doctor
m: To refuse to acknowledge or address a problem because you are afraid of the consequences of solving it.
s: When someone has a serious issue at work but refuses to talk to their manager about it because they fear getting in trouble. When a person knows they have a health problem but won't see a doctor because they're afraid of what the diagnosis might be.

l: avoid and conceal as if very deep
m: To keep something secret or hidden with extreme care, refusing to disclose it under any circumstances.
s: When someone refuses to talk about an embarrassing mistake they made at work. When a company tries very hard to hide information about product defects from the public. When a person keeps their personal problems completely private and won't discuss them with anyone.

m: To award people based on the merits and contributions they have made.
s: After a successful project, the manager needs to decide who gets bonuses by looking at each person's actual work and results. When a company promotes employees, they should consider their actual achievements and performance rather than favoritism or personal relationships.

m: To empathize with someone by imagining yourself in their circumstances and understanding their perspective and feelings.
s: When you're angry at a friend but then realize they were under a lot of stress. When a parent finally understands why their teenage child made a certain decision after thinking about how they felt at that age.

l: criticize the head and evaluate the feet
m: To nitpick someone's appearance or find fault with every aspect of how they look.
s: When someone is being overly critical of another person's physical appearance, commenting on everything from their hairstyle to their shoes. When people gather to gossip and make judgmental remarks about how someone looks or dresses.

p: shí shí wù zhě wéi jùn jié
l: Those who understand the demands of the times are considered outstanding talents
m: A wise and capable person is one who recognizes current circumstances and adapts their actions accordingly rather than stubbornly clinging to outdated approaches.
s: When a business owner shifts their strategy to match changing market conditions instead of refusing to evolve. When someone abandons an ineffective plan and adopts a better approach after assessing the current situation.

l: old horse that knows the way
m: An experienced person who can guide others through a difficult situation because they have been through it before.
s: When you need advice from someone who has done something many times before. When a veteran employee shows a new worker how to handle a tricky client or process. When an experienced friend helps you navigate a problem they've already solved.

l: words do not reach the meaning
m: One's words fail to fully express or convey what one truly intends or feels.
s: When you try to explain a complex idea but the words just don't come out right and people misunderstand you. When someone writes an email trying to apologize but their message comes across wrong and makes things worse instead of better.

m: Language or writing that is so convoluted, awkward, and difficult to understand that it obscures rather than clarifies meaning.
s: When reading a legal document or academic paper so poorly written that you have to read each sentence multiple times to understand it. When someone explains something in such a confusing and roundabout way that it's harder to understand than the original concept.

m: To act with genuine sincerity and honest intentions, without deception or hidden motives.
s: When someone apologizes and you can tell they really mean it. When a person makes a serious promise and you believe they will keep it because their words and actions match. When someone helps you without expecting anything in return.

m: To feel extremely anxious, apprehensive, and respectful, often when facing someone of higher authority or status.
s: When you're about to meet your boss to discuss a serious mistake you made at work. When a student nervously approaches their teacher to ask for an extension on an assignment, feeling very sorry and worried about the request.

l: punishment and extraction know no satiation
m: Excessive and insatiable demands for taxes, tribute, or extortion that never end no matter how much is taken.
s: When a corrupt official keeps raising taxes on the people even though they are already suffering. When a company keeps increasing prices and fees on customers without any limit or justification.

l: root out those of a different mind
m: To eliminate or suppress anyone who opposes you or holds different opinions, especially through ruthless and authoritarian means.
s: When a leader fires or punishes all employees who disagree with their decisions. When a dictator removes anyone from power who doesn't share their ideology. When someone in authority systematically removes all critics and rivals to maintain control.

p: huà bù tóu jī bàn jù duō
l: When words do not match, half a sentence is already too many
m: When two people's thoughts and feelings are incompatible, even minimal conversation is pointless or uncomfortable.
s: When you're trying to explain something to someone who fundamentally disagrees with you and you realize further discussion is futile. When two people have nothing in common and any attempt at conversation feels awkward and forced.

m: Someone who is deceitful and uses many different tricks and schemes to achieve their goals.
s: When a con artist uses different manipulation tactics to cheat people out of money. When a politician constantly uses deception and underhanded tactics to gain power. When a colleague keeps scheming in various ways to sabotage your work.

m: To speak in a disorganized and incoherent manner without clear logical order or structure.
s: When someone is so nervous or flustered during a presentation that their words come out jumbled and hard to follow. When a person is extremely upset or drunk and can't form coherent sentences. When someone tries to explain something but their thoughts are all over the place and nothing makes sense.

m: To speak in vague, unclear, or incomplete terms without providing sufficient explanation or clarity.
s: When someone gives you instructions but leaves out important details and you're confused about what to do. When a teacher explains a concept but skips over the key points and students don't understand it. When a person tells a story but glosses over the crucial parts that would make sense of the whole thing.

m: Speaking with sincere concern and deep feeling, offering earnest advice that comes from genuine care for another person.
s: When a parent gives their child serious advice about life choices, speaking slowly and carefully to make sure they understand how much they care. When an older mentor sits down with a younger person to warn them about making a serious mistake, their tone showing they truly want to help.

m: To teach others, especially young people, in a way that harms their development or leads them down the wrong path.
s: When a teacher gives students terrible advice that ruins their future prospects. When an older person teaches a young person bad habits or morals that negatively impact their life.

m: To be led astray or to deviate from the correct path, whether literally or morally, often resulting in negative consequences.
s: When a young person falls in with the wrong crowd and starts engaging in criminal behavior. When someone abandons their principles and starts doing things they know are wrong because of bad influences.

l: entice the enemy to advance deeply
m: A military strategy of deliberately retreating or appearing weak to draw the enemy far from their base and supply lines, making them vulnerable to counterattack.
s: When a business competitor pulls back from a market, only to launch a surprise comeback when their rival overextends. When a chess player sacrifices material to lure their opponent's pieces into an unfavorable position where they can be trapped or defeated.

m: To teach others with patience and dedication, never tiring of the effort to help people learn and improve.
s: When a teacher stays late after school to help struggling students understand difficult concepts. When a mentor continuously guides someone through their career development without getting frustrated or giving up.

m: Content or behavior that encourages or instructs others in immoral or criminal conduct such as theft and sexual misconduct.
s: When a book or movie glorifies criminal activity and seems designed to corrupt young people's morals. When someone's actions or words serve as a bad example that encourages others to behave immorally or illegally.

l: speak once without a second word
m: One's word is absolute and cannot be changed or contradicted once spoken.
s: When a boss makes a decision and won't listen to any objections or alternative suggestions. When a parent sets a rule and refuses to negotiate or reconsider it no matter what the child says.

m: To follow through on what you say and actually do what you promise.
s: When someone makes a commitment and actually keeps it, like a friend who says they'll help you move and shows up on time with a truck. When a manager promises a raise and actually gives it to you.

p: shuō cáo cāo ， cáo cāo jiù dào
l: Speak of Cao Cao and Cao Cao arrives
m: When you mention someone and they suddenly appear or something happens immediately after you mention it, as if by coincidence.
s: You're talking about how you haven't seen your old friend in years, and suddenly they text you. You're complaining about how quiet your boss has been, and right then they walk into the room.

l: speaking of it the story is long
m: There is too much history or context to explain everything in detail right now.
s: When someone asks why you and your friend stopped talking, and you don't want to get into all the complicated backstory. When a coworker asks why a project failed and there were many contributing factors that would take forever to fully explain.

m: To gossip or engage in idle talk, often making critical or negative comments about others behind their backs.

m: To give someone sincere, repeated warnings or advice with the intention of helping them avoid mistakes or harm.

When a boss asks an employee to complete an impossible task by tomorrow as if it's no big deal.

m: To speak in a way that is understated yet penetrating, delivering profound truths through seemingly simple or modest language.

m: To make witty remarks or jokes that are sharp and pointed but are not intended to cause real harm or hurt feelings.
s: When someone makes a clever joke at your expense but you know they mean well and there's no ill intent behind it. When a friend teases you in a funny way that's meant to be lighthearted rather than hurtful.

m: An expression of gratitude or relief that something fortunate has happened or a difficult situation has been resolved.
s: When you finally finish a difficult exam and are relieved it's over. When someone you were worried about contacts you to say they're safe after an accident.

m: To remain modest in attitude and careful in one's actions, avoiding arrogance and recklessness.
s: When someone achieves success but doesn't brag about it and continues to work diligently. When a leader listens to others' opinions and doesn't make hasty decisions. When a student does well in school but stays grounded and keeps studying hard without becoming overconfident.

m: A person of noble character who is humble, courteous, and virtuous in conduct and bearing.
s: When describing someone who is well-mannered and humble despite their success or high status. When you want to praise someone for being gracious and not arrogant even though they have every reason to be.

l: cautious in small matters and careful in subtle details
m: To be extremely careful and cautious in all one's actions, even in small or trivial matters, showing excessive worry about making mistakes.
s: When someone is overly worried about every tiny detail and takes forever to make simple decisions. When a coworker is so afraid of doing anything wrong that they become paralyzed and can't get their work done efficiently.

m: One should be prudent and circumspect in both what they say and how they act, avoiding recklessness and potential harm.
s: When someone needs to be very careful about what they say in a sensitive business meeting or around authority figures. When a person is in a delicate social situation and needs to avoid offending anyone or making a mistake.

m: Incorrect ideas or false information spread widely and become accepted as truth.

m: To suddenly achieve a complete understanding or breakthrough after a period of confusion or struggle.
s: When you've been struggling to understand a difficult math concept and then suddenly it all makes sense. When someone has been confused about how to solve a problem at work, but then has a sudden realization that clears everything up. When you finally grasp the deeper meaning of something you've read or studied multiple times before.

m: To have a broad, tolerant perspective and generous spirit that allows one to overlook minor offenses and not hold grudges.

m: A passionate and determined spirit combined with lofty, noble ambitions and ideals.
s: When someone is young and full of energy, dreaming big about changing the world or achieving great things. When a person expresses their determination to accomplish something remarkable and meaningful in life, speaking with genuine passion and conviction.

m: Boastful or exaggerated claims and promises made with great confidence, often without the ability to back them up.
s: When someone makes grand promises about what they'll accomplish but never follows through. When a politician gives a rousing speech full of ambitious claims that sound impressive but are unrealistic.

l: the leopard dies and leaves its skin

When someone does something notable that will have a lasting impact on how history views them.

l: carry thorns and ask for punishment

s: When someone has wronged another person and genuinely wants to make amends by apologizing and accepting whatever consequences come. When a friend or colleague takes full responsibility for their error and shows they are willing to face the consequences to repair the relationship.

l: bear heavy burdens to reach distant destinations
m: To endure hardship and carry heavy responsibilities in order to achieve long-term goals or success.

l: rely on a corner and stubbornly resist
m: To stubbornly resist or refuse to surrender even when in a desperate or cornered position with no hope of victory.

When a criminal refuses to surrender to police even though they're surrounded with no escape.

m: One bears an inescapable responsibility that cannot be delegated or avoided.
s: When a parent must care for their elderly parents regardless of personal circumstances. When a team leader knows they are ultimately accountable for their team's failures, even if others made the mistakes.

m: Everyone bears responsibility according to their role and duty; accountability should be assigned to those who are actually responsible.
s: When a project fails and you need to figure out who was supposed to be in charge. When someone tries to blame others for a mistake that was clearly their job to prevent. When you're dividing tasks among team members and need to make clear who is accountable for what.

m: Someone who has suffered a major failure or defeat and has lost credibility or authority as a result.
s: When a sports team loses a championship game, the coach might be treated as a defeated general by critics. When a company's CEO makes a bad business decision that causes the company to fail, they become a defeated general in the eyes of investors and employees.

m: Something is authentic, of high quality, and fairly priced without deception or exaggeration.
s: When you buy a product and it's exactly as advertised, with no hidden flaws or misleading marketing. When a friend recommends a restaurant and the food is delicious and the prices are reasonable, not overpriced.

l: cast doubt and pose difficult questions
m: To question something critically and challenge it with tough, probing inquiries in order to test its validity or expose weaknesses.
s: When a journalist aggressively questions a politician's claims during a press conference to verify the facts. When a student challenges their teacher's explanation by asking pointed questions that expose logical inconsistencies. When a skeptical colleague demands evidence and scrutinizes every detail of a colleague's proposal before accepting it.

m: To be excessively driven by desire for money, material gain, and social position.
s: When someone abandons their principles or betrays friends just to make more money or climb the social ladder. When a person is willing to do anything unethical as long as it leads to financial success and prestige.

l: greedily claim the credit of heaven
m: To arrogantly take credit for something that is due to fortune, nature, or circumstances beyond one's control rather than acknowledging one's actual contribution.
s: When someone takes full credit for a successful project that succeeded mostly due to luck or timing. When a leader claims personal achievement for results that were actually achieved by their team's hard work.

m: Being greedy for minor gains causes you to lose much larger and more important things.
s: When someone refuses a good job offer because the starting salary is slightly lower, then misses out on a career that would have made them wealthy. When a business owner cuts corners to save a small amount of money on materials, but ends up losing customers and their reputation because the quality suffers.

m: Having insatiable greed that is never content with what one already possesses.
s: When a wealthy person keeps wanting more money and status despite already having plenty. When someone receives a gift but immediately complains it's not expensive enough or asks for something better.

m: The abuse of power for personal gain combined with a decline in moral standards and integrity.
s: When officials take bribes and embezzle public funds. When someone in a position of authority becomes increasingly dishonest and unethical over time, abandoning their principles for personal wealth and power.

l: greedy for life, afraid of death
m: An excessive attachment to survival that leads someone to act shamefully or betray their principles to avoid danger.
s: When a soldier abandons his comrades to save himself in battle. When someone refuses to stand up for what's right because they're too scared of the consequences. When a person would rather live dishonorably than face any real risk or hardship.

l: greed for bribes and perversion of law
m: Officials or those in power accept bribes and abuse their authority by twisting the law for personal gain.
s: When a corrupt judge accepts money to rule in favor of a guilty defendant. When a government official takes kickbacks from contractors in exchange for awarding them lucrative contracts. When police officers extort money from citizens and ignore actual crimes.

m: Having a glib, sharp tongue that is prone to making cutting remarks, insults, or scurrilous comments without regard for others' feelings.
s: When someone is always making sarcastic jokes at other people's expense. When a person has a tendency to say mean or insulting things casually, as if they don't realize how hurtful their words are.

p: pín wú lì zhuī zhī dì
l: poor without even a place to stand an awl
m: So poor that one owns no land whatsoever, not even a tiny piece of ground.
s: When describing someone in extreme poverty who is homeless or owns absolutely nothing. When talking about a refugee or displaced person who has lost all their possessions and property.

m: A person is suffering from the combined hardship of both extreme poverty and serious illness at the same time.
s: When someone loses their job and then gets diagnosed with a serious disease requiring expensive treatment. When an elderly person has no savings and falls gravely ill, unable to afford medical care. When a family is already struggling financially and then a major health crisis strikes a family member.

l: expend effort but gain no favor
m: To work hard at something but receive no appreciation, gratitude, or positive results for your effort.
s: When you help someone repeatedly but they never say thank you or acknowledge your help. When you put in extra work on a project but your boss doesn't recognize or appreciate your contribution.

m: To go to great lengths and exert maximum effort, often through cunning or clever planning, to achieve a goal.
s: When someone spends weeks carefully planning and strategizing to win a promotion or seal a business deal. When a person devises an elaborate scheme to convince their parents to let them go on a trip they really want to take.

l: leave people with material for speech
m: To provide others with a legitimate reason or evidence to criticize, blame, or speak badly of you.
s: When you do something careless or wrong that gives your enemies ammunition to attack you. When someone acts improperly in public and then gets criticized for it, they've given people cause for complaint. If you make a mistake at work, you're giving your boss legitimate grounds to question your competence.

m: To cause damage or problems that will have lasting negative consequences far into the future.
s: When a company makes a poor decision today that will hurt their business for years to come. When a parent's bad habits negatively influence their children for generations. When a government policy creates long-term societal problems that are hard to fix.

l: bequeath laughter to the great masters
m: To do something so foolish or shameful that one becomes a laughingstock before knowledgeable or sophisticated people.
s: When someone makes a ridiculous public mistake and embarrasses themselves in front of experts or important people. When you act in such an unprofessional way that you become the object of ridicule among your peers or superiors.

l: lock the door after the thief has left
m: Taking preventive measures only after damage has already been done is ineffective and pointless.
s: When a company finally implements security measures only after being hacked. When someone decides to save money after they've already spent all their savings on unnecessary things. When a person starts exercising and eating healthy only after they've already developed serious health problems.

l: The thief cries catch the thief
m: To accuse others of wrongdoing in order to divert attention from or cover up one's own guilt or misconduct.
s: When someone who is guilty of a crime accuses an innocent person to avoid suspicion. When a corrupt official blames their subordinates for crimes they themselves committed to protect their reputation.

m: To behave in a sneaky, furtive manner that suggests dishonest or criminal intent.
s: When someone is acting suspiciously or trying to hide something, looking around nervously before doing something. When a person moves around in a stealthy way or has a guilty, evasive demeanor that makes you think they're up to no good.

m: Corruption and bribery occur openly and brazenly without concealment or shame.
s: When officials openly accept bribes without fear of consequences. When a workplace where gifts and favors are used to gain unfair advantages and everyone just accepts it as normal. When a system is so corrupt that people no longer bother to hide their unethical dealings.

l: pleasing to the heart and delighting to the eye
m: Something is so beautiful or well-arranged that it brings joy and satisfaction to both the mind and the senses.
s: When you walk into a beautifully decorated room that makes you feel happy and calm. When you see a stunning sunset or a perfectly arranged garden that makes you feel peaceful and content.

m: Justice requires that good conduct be rewarded and wrongdoing be punished fairly and consistently without favoritism.
s: When a manager praises employees who work hard and disciplines those who slack off equally, showing no bias. When a school gives prizes to top students and detention to troublemakers based on clear, consistent rules. When a coach rewards good performance and benches underperforming players without playing favorites.

p: péi le fū rén yòu zhé bīng
l: lost the lady and also lost the soldiers

m: To praise someone or something continuously and enthusiastically without stopping.
s: When a friend tries a new restaurant and can't stop talking about how amazing the food was. When your parents keep bragging about your accomplishments to all their friends.

l: red earth for a thousand miles
m: A vast area of land that has become completely barren and desolate, typically due to drought, famine, or disaster.

m: A pure, innocent, and sincere heart untainted by cynicism or selfishness, like that of a newborn baby.

m: Sincere and unwavering loyalty and devotion, showing genuine courage and commitment to a person or cause.

m: Someone or something is extremely well-known and widely recognized for their prominence or achievements.

m: To be in a desperate situation with no way out, having exhausted all options and resources.

l: go to boiling water and step into fire
m: to brave extreme danger or hardship without hesitation; to be willing to sacrifice oneself for a cause.
s: When someone is willing to do anything dangerous to help a friend in desperate need. When a soldier charges into battle knowing the odds are against them. When a parent would face any peril to protect their child.

l: drive to exhaustion and kill completely
m: To destroy someone or something entirely without leaving any survivors or remnants, showing no mercy or restraint.
s: When a powerful person or group completely eliminates their enemies and leaves nothing behind. When someone is determined to wipe out a problem entirely rather than just reduce it. When a company aggressively crushes all competition in their market.

m: A structural framework describing the four essential stages of narrative development: opening, development, climax, and resolution.

l: bring the dead back to life
m: To save someone or something from a hopeless situation and restore it to a state of vitality or success.

m: To take advantage of someone's misfortune or crisis to exploit them for personal gain.

m: Take action promptly when conditions are favorable, before the opportunity passes or circumstances change.

l: surpassing the extraordinary and exceeding the sacred

s: When describing a musician or artist whose work is so brilliant it seems almost impossibly perfect. When someone demonstrates abilities that seem to transcend what normal humans are capable of achieving.

l: transcend the dust and rise above the common
m: To surpass ordinary worldly concerns and achieve a state of spiritual or intellectual elevation beyond the common person.
s: When someone dedicates themselves to artistic or philosophical pursuits and seems detached from material concerns. When a person demonstrates exceptional wisdom or moral character that sets them apart from average society.

l: transcend and remain outside material things
m: To rise above worldly concerns and material pursuits, maintaining a detached and spiritual perspective on life.
s: When someone doesn't care about money or status and focuses only on personal growth or inner peace. When a person remains calm and unaffected by gossip, drama, or social competition around them.

l: surpass the crowd and exceed peers
m: To be extraordinarily superior to others in a particular skill or quality, standing far above comparison.
s: When someone's talent or ability is so exceptional that nobody else comes close to their level. When describing an athlete, artist, or professional whose performance is unmatched by their contemporaries.

m: to overstep one's authority or position by interfering in matters that are not one's responsibility.
s: When a manager starts doing the work of their team members instead of delegating. When someone keeps giving unsolicited advice about how others should handle their own business or personal affairs.

m: People rush to pursue or seek something with enthusiasm and without hesitation, often without considering whether it is worthwhile.
s: When a new trendy restaurant opens and everyone immediately crowds in without even knowing if the food is good. When people eagerly buy the latest smartphone model the moment it's released, even though the previous version was perfectly fine.

l: pursue warmth and attach to power
m: to curry favor with those in power and influential people by flattering them and seeking their patronage.

s: When someone is uncertain about pursuing a goal and keeps second-guessing themselves instead of moving forward decisively. When a project keeps hitting obstacles and the team struggles to maintain progress without losing motivation.

m: Someone who is intelligent, clever, and full of brilliant ideas and strategies.
s: When describing a leader who always has a smart plan to solve difficult problems. When praising someone for their ability to think creatively and come up with effective solutions in challenging situations.

m: To conduct oneself with excessive pride and arrogance, displaying haughtiness and disdain toward others.
s: When someone who just got a promotion suddenly starts acting superior to their colleagues and looking down on them. When a student wins a competition and begins treating their classmates as inferiors, refusing to associate with them.

m: To be eager and excited about trying something new or proving one's abilities.
s: When someone is really enthusiastic about participating in a competition or activity they've never done before. When a friend is visibly excited and impatient to test out a new skill or challenge themselves.

l: traverse mountains and wade through water
m: To travel through difficult terrain and harsh conditions, often implying a long and arduous journey.

When reflecting on how someone you thought was trustworthy eventually showed their true nature through their actions over months or years.

m: A despicable person of no real importance who acts arrogantly and tries to cause trouble despite their insignificance.
s: When a minor political figure tries to stir up conflict and make headlines despite having little real power or influence. When someone unimportant keeps trying to challenge or provoke you, thinking they matter more than they actually do.

m: To be indecisive or uncertain and therefore unable to move forward or take action.

m: Feeling extremely proud and satisfied with oneself, often excessively so, while contemplating future success or accomplishments.
s: When someone has just achieved a success and is walking around feeling overly pleased with themselves. When a person struts confidently after completing a project, convinced they've done better than anyone else could have done.

m: To be indecisive and hesitant, unable to move forward due to doubt or uncertainty.
s: When someone is standing at a crossroads in their career but keeps second-guessing themselves and can't make a decision. m: One problem is barely fixed before another more serious one appears, or difficulties keep multiplying faster than they can be solved.
s: When you patch one hole in your clothes only to have another tear appear immediately. When a company fixes one software bug but two new ones emerge, making the situation worse overall.

l: tread the worn path and follow old ways

m: to waste or squander precious time, especially during one's youth or prime years, through idleness or lack of purpose.

m: To be unable to control one's own actions or choices due to external circumstances or forces beyond one's will.
s: When someone is forced to do something against their wishes because of circumstances they cannot escape. When a person is constrained by obligations, peer pressure, or external constraints that leave them powerless to act freely.

m: To feel as though you are physically present in a place or situation, experiencing it directly as if you were truly there.

m: One's value, status, or reputation has increased dramatically, often suddenly or as a result of a significant achievement or event.

m: To practice what you preach by demonstrating commitment through personal example and direct participation rather than just words.
s: When a teacher not only teaches students about exercise but goes to the gym themselves to show they live a healthy lifestyle. When a leader asks their team to work hard and then stays late to work alongside them on the project.

m: A leader demonstrates courage and commitment by taking action before asking others to do the same, setting an example through personal involvement rather than just giving orders.
s: When a manager works the same long hours they expect from their team during a crisis. When a coach runs alongside their athletes during training rather than just watching from the sidelines. When a parent is the first to try a difficult task they're encouraging their child to attempt.

p: shēn zài fú zhōng bù zhī fú
l: Being in fortune but not knowing fortune
m: To be in a fortunate situation but fail to appreciate or recognize the blessings one possesses.
s: When someone has a comfortable life with loving family and steady job but constantly complains about minor problems. When a person with good health and financial stability doesn't realize how lucky they are compared to others facing real hardship.

m: Material possessions and worldly goods are ultimately temporary and unimportant compared to one's life and integrity.
s: When someone is willing to sacrifice their health or reputation for money. When a person realizes that losing their job or possessions isn't as important as their relationships and well-being.

m: To be in excellent physical condition with robust health and great strength.
